title: Monkeys May Share Our Instinct for Geometry, Study Finds
summary: What if you found out a monkey could think about shapes almost the same way you do? That's what a new study suggests. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University compared how preschool kids, two monkey species, and adults from Bolivia and Namibia matched shapes and angles in computer games. The adults belonged to the Tsimane' and Himba communities, where people don't study geometry in school. The monkeys — rhesus monkeys in a lab and olive baboons in a zoo — played for treats like fruit cereal. Preschoolers played for stickers, but weren't always easy to convince. "Sometimes kids reject you," said cognitive neuroscientist Jialin Li. "You have to bargain with them." One baboon, Kalamata, became an avid gamer, playing for hours a day. The team even built a "Primate Portal" — a cabin inside the baboon enclosure where a scientist runs games on a screen. The big question: do all these minds think about shapes the same way? To find out, researchers compared each group's mistakes to two computer models that mimic different ways of thinking. Monkeys and humans made similar errors, hinting their minds process shapes similarly. "Humans are not unique in this," Li concluded, "but we are better." Not everyone is convinced. Moira Dillon of New York University notes that computer models aren't real minds, and scientists can't see inside a monkey's head. Véronique Izard of the University of Paris Cité wonders if different models might reveal differences the study missed. Still, the research opens exciting questions about how geometric thinking evolved — and elementary schoolers are now designing new games for the baboons.
why_it_matters: Figuring out which kinds of thinking come built into the brain and which come from school and culture shapes how math is taught — and how people decide which minds deserve respect.

background_read: Carnegie Mellon University (a research university in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, known for its psychology and computer science departments) ran the study with children, adults, and monkeys.

The Tsimane' (an Indigenous people who live in the Bolivian Amazon) and the Himba (a herding people of northern Namibia) grow up without geometry lessons, which is why researchers compare them with schooled children to test whether shape skills are built into the brain.

The idea that some math intuitions are inborn is old: the ancient Greek mathematician Euclid wrote the first famous rulebook for geometry more than two thousand years ago, and other studies have found basic shape sense in babies and in animals.
Rhesus monkeys and olive baboons are primates — the animal group that includes monkeys, apes, and humans — so scientists study them to learn which mental skills we share with our closest relatives.
Skeptics point out that a computer model is only a simplified program, so it can stand in for a real brain but never replace one.

perspectives.description: The study's authors say the matching error patterns hint that monkeys and humans process shapes in similar ways, so geometry may rest on very old mental machinery rather than only on schooling. For them, the finding widens the circle of minds that can do real mathematics.

Critics like Moira Dillon argue that computer models are not minds, so matching a model's mistakes proves less than it seems. They also note that a monkey's inner experience cannot be observed directly, and that different test rewards could affect how each group plays.

The design follows a long tradition of testing people with little formal schooling — such as Amazonian and Namibian communities — to separate culture from biology. Whatever the outcome, cross-cultural and cross-species comparisons remain the main tool for asking whether math is invented or discovered.

The team is already handing the next round of game design to elementary schoolers, which could make animal testing more animal-friendly and more creative. Better brain-imaging tools could one day replace guesswork about what a monkey is thinking.
